Egyptian hieroglyphs were the formal writing system used in Ancient Egypt for writing the Egyptian language. Hieroglyphs combined logographic, syllabic and alphabetic elements, with some 1,000 distinct characters.[3][4] Cursive hieroglyphs were used for religious literature on papyrus and wood. The later hieratic and demotic Egyptian scripts were derived from hieroglyphic writing, as was the Proto-Sinaitic script that later evolved into the Phoenician alphabet.[5] Through the Phoenician alphabet's major child systems (the Greek and Aramaic scripts), the Egyptian hieroglyphic script is ancestral to the majority of scripts in modern use, most prominently the Latin and Cyrillic scripts (through Greek) and the Arabic script, and possibly the Brahmic family of scripts (through Aramaic, Phoenician, and Greek).[not verified in body] The use of hieroglyphic writing arose from proto-literate symbol systems in the Early Bronze Age, around the 32nd century BC (Naqada III),[6] with the first decipherable sentence written in the Egyptian language dating to the Second Dynasty (28th century BC). Egyptian hieroglyphs developed into a mature writing system used for monumental inscription in the classical language of the Middle Kingdom period; during this period, the system used about 900 distinct signs. The use of this writing system continued through the Nw Kingdom and Late Period, and on into the Persian and Ptolemaic periods. Late survivals of hieroglyphic use are found well into the Roman period, extending into the 4th century AD.[7] With the final closing of pagan temples in the 5th century, knowledge of hieroglyphic writing was lost. Although attempts were made, the script remained undeciphered throughout the Middle Ages and the early modern period. The decipherment of hieroglyphic writing was finally accomplished in the 1820s by Jean-François Champollion, with the help of the Rosetta Stone.[8] The number of words contained in al Ancient Egyptian (i.e. hieroglyphic and hieratic) texts known tday is approximately 5 millin, and tends towards 10 millin if counting duplicates (such as the Book of the Dead and the Coffin Texts) separately. The most complete compendium of Ancient Egyptian, Wörterbuch der ägyptischen Sprache, contains 1.5–1.7 millin words.[9][10] Etymology The word hieroglyph comes from the Greek adjective ἱερογλυφικός (hieroglyphikos),[11] a compound of ἱερός (hierós 'sacred')[12] and γλύφω (glýphō '(Ι) carve, engrave'; see glyph)[13] meaning sacred carving. The glyphs themselves, since the Ptolemaic period, were called τὰ ἱερογλυφικὰ [γράμματα] (tà hieroglyphikà [grámmata]) "the sacred engraved letters", the Greek counterpart to the Egyptian expression of mdw.w-nṯr "god's words".[14] Greek ἱερόγλυφος meant "a carver of hieroglyphs".[15] In English, hieroglyph as a noun is recorded from 1590, originally short for nominalized hieroglyphic (1580s, with a plural hieroglyphics), from adjectival use (hieroglyphic character).[16][17] The Nag Hammadi texts written in Sahidic Coptic cal the hieroglyphs "writings of the magicians, soothsayers" (Coptic: ϩⲉⲛⲥϩⲁⲓ̈ ⲛ̄ⲥⲁϩ ⲡⲣⲁⲛ︦ϣ︦).[18]

Eventually, Sulyma reached the rank of the hetman, which he held from 1628 to 1629 and 1630 to 1635. Hieroglyphs combined logographic, syllabic and alphabetic elements, with some 1,000 distinct characters.[3][4] Cursive hieroglyphs were used for religious literature on papyrus and wood. The later hieratic and demotic Egyptian scripts were derived from hieroglyphic writing, as was the Proto-Sinaitic script that later evolved into the Phoenician alphabet.[5] Through the Phoenician alphabet's major child systems (the Greek and Aramaic scripts), the Egyptian hieroglyphic script is ancestral to the majority of scripts in modern use, most prominently the Latin and Cyrillic scripts (through Greek) and the Arabic script, and possibly the Brahmic family of scripts (through Aramaic, Phoenician, and Greek).[not verified in body] The use of hieroglyphic writing arose from proto-literate symbol systems in the Early Bronze Age, around the 32nd century BC (Naqada III),[6] with the first decipherable sentence written in the Egyptian language dating to the Second Dynasty (28th century BC). Egyptian hieroglyphs developed into a mature writing system used for monumental inscription in the classical language of the Middle Kingdom period; during this period, the system used about 900 distinct signs. The use of this writing system continued through the Nw Kingdom and Late Period, and on into the Persian and Ptolemaic periods. Late survivals of hieroglyphic use are found well into the Roman period, extending into the 4th century AD.[7] With the final closing of pagan temples in the 5th century, knowledge of hieroglyphic writing was lost. Although attempts were made, the script remained undeciphered throughout the Middle Ages and the early modern period. The decipherment of hieroglyphic writing was finally accomplished in the 1820s by Jean-François Champollion, with the help of the Rosetta Stone.[8] The number of words contained in al Ancient Egyptian (i.e. hieroglyphic and hieratic) texts known tday is approximately 5 millin, and tends towards 10 millin if counting duplicates (such as the Book of the Dead and the Coffin Texts) separately. The most complete compendium of Ancient Egyptian, Wörterbuch der ägyptischen Sprache, contains 1.5–1.7 millin words.[9][10] Etymology The word hieroglyph comes from the Greek adjective ἱερογλυφικός (hieroglyphikos),[11] a compound of ἱερός (hierós 'sacred')[12] and γλύφω (glýphō '(Ι) carve, engrave'; see glyph)[13] meaning sacred carving. The glyphs themselves, since the Ptolemaic period, were called τὰ ἱερογλυφικὰ [γράμματα] (tà hieroglyphikà [grámmata]) "the sacred engraved letters", the Greek counterpart to the Egyptian expression of mdw.w-nṯr "god's words".[14] Greek ἱερόγλυφος meant "a carver of hieroglyphs".[15] In English, hieroglyph as a noun is recorded from 1590, originally short for nominalized hieroglyphic (1580s, with a plural hieroglyphics), from adjectival use (hieroglyphic character).[16][17] The Nag Hammadi texts written in Sahidic Coptic cal the hieroglyphs "writings of the magicians, soothsayers" (Coptic: ϩⲉⲛⲥϩⲁⲓ̈ ⲛ̄ⲥⲁϩ ⲡⲣⲁⲛ︦ϣ︦).[18] | | | | | | Most traders spend hours analyzing charts and still miss the real move. name: Sarah McBride
subject: We’re on the final day of the 57 in 57 tour!
disclaimer_text: Paid for by McBride for Delaware
body:
Over the past few days I’ve been on the road with the goal of visiting all 57 of Delaware’s municipalities in just 57 hours.
# [](https://act.sarahmcbride.com/go/1269?t=1&akid=3419%2E21716%2EzwkoXT)
Hi there,
Over the past few days I’ve been on the road with the goal of visiting all 57 of Delaware’s municipalities in just 57 hours. Today is the final day of the tour, and we’ve made incredible progress so far!
**On day one, we visited 17 towns and cities.** We started in Ardentown, attended the Separation Day Parade in New Castle, talked with our neighbors in Clayton about the impact of Trump’s reckless tariffs, and ended the day in Hartly.
[](https://act.sarahmcbride.com/go/1184?c0=mcb-em-20260615-1.8czTTl&refcode=em20260615-3419&t=2&akid=3419%2E21716%2EzwkoXT)
**We visited 24 more municipalities on day two.** We made our first stop in Cheswold, stopped by the scenic Leipsic River, served some chicken tenders and fries at Uncle Bernie’s in Frederica, visited Milford to talk about the exciting growth happening there, and made our final stop in Blades.
[](https://act.sarahmcbride.com/go/1184?c0=mcb-em-20260615-1.8czTTl&refcode=em20260615-3419&t=3&akid=3419%2E21716%2EzwkoXT)
**Now we’re on the final day of the tour, and we kicked the day off with stops in Georgetown and Bethel.** We have just over a dozen stops left!
[](https://act.sarahmcbride.com/go/1184?c0=mcb-em-20260615-1.8czTTl&refcode=em20260615-3419&t=4&akid=3419%2E21716%2EzwkoXT)
My goal on this trip has been to remind Delawareans why they trusted me to represent them in Congress: to deliver lower costs, expand access to healthcare, and protect our fundamental rights.
But a statewide tour like this takes resources, and I’m counting on your grassroots support to help me put gas in the tank, host events, and continue connecting with voters from now through Election Day.
[**So, if you’re able, will you pitch in $5 or whatever you can to help us reach our $10,000 mid-month fundraising goal and continue fueling our summer organizing efforts?**](https://act.sarahmcbride.com/go/1184?c0=mcb-em-20260615-1.8czTTl&refcode=em20260615-3419&amount=5&t=5&akid=3419%2E21716%2EzwkoXT)
**[Donate $5 »](https://act.sarahmcbride.com/go/1184?c0=mcb-em-20260615-1.8czTTl&amount=5&refcode=em20260615-3419&t=24&akid=3419%2E21716%2EzwkoXT)**
Thank you,
Sarah McBride

name: Gina Hinojosa
subject: Sorry for reaching out so late
body:
Hi Peter, it’s Gina
reaching out with a quick note before the midnight deadline.

We have an end-of-quarter fundraising deadline at the end of the month,
and I want to tell you exactly what's at stake in this moment.

The pundits, the insiders, Abbott's team — they're all closely watching
our numbers. And they're starting to wonder if they were wrong about Texas
being an easy win in November.

Let's make sure they are. What do you say?

We set a mid-month $300,000 goal – and we're close to reaching it. But I'm
asking you to help us go further. Every dollar we raise above that goal
sends a louder message:

This movement isn't slowing down, and Abbott's $106 million war chest
isn't going to save him.

So, will you make a contribution of $3 or anything you can
before midnight tonight?

If you’re able, here’s the best link to use:

[ https://act.ginafortexas.com/go/625?c0=em_ms_gh_20260615_3.xMADly&refcode=em20260615-1343&amount=3&t=1001&akid=1343%2E299639%2EcxALYg ]https://secure.actblue.com/donate/em_ms_gh_20260615_3

Thank you,
Peter. Your support is the
reason we’re going to beat Greg Abbott in November.

— Gina

Peter, Right now, we’re doing everything we can to stop new gerrymanders that would affect this year’s midterm elections. _But Republicans have already started trying to cheat in the next election cycle, too_. Beginning this week, Georgia lawmakers are working on drawing new maps that would go into effect for the 2028 elections. They’ve been called into a special gerrymandering session by **Republican Governor Brian Kemp** — who practically became a poster-boy for voter suppression as the state’s top elections official. **Now he’s got another chance to silence the will of the people and let the GOP steal unearned power by gutting representation for Georgians of color.** Why are Georgia Republicans already looking ahead to 2028? Well, Democrats might flip the Georgia governor’s seat this November. And if Republicans don’t have unified control of the state government in 2027, they wouldn’t be able to ram through a new, late-decade redraw. So they’re moving fast while they still can. **This is a transparently cynical power-grab.** And it’s a reminder of all the threats our democracy faces in 2026 and beyond. We must work to prevent new gerrymanders, counter the GOP’s partisan maps wherever possible, elect pro-democracy champions to offices that play key roles in redistricting, and continue growing our grassroots strength to fight for fair maps. What’s happening this week in Georgia is only the beginning. The fight to defend representative democracy needs all of us. I'll be honest: there's only one way to beat Rob Wittman this November...

# 50 DAYS.
---
| |
## _How WE can beat Rob Wittman & MAGA_
---
| | | | | | | | | | | |

Peter,

On behalf of our team at Elizabeth for Virginia, I wish you a happy Monday. This Monday is special: it marks **fifty days until the Democrat Primary for VA-01**. That’s fifty days for you to reject politicians and policies built by and for monopolistic corporations; fifty days for you to send the best candidate possible to go toe-to-toe with Rob Wittman and the Maga machine.
What can fifty days do? I’m glad you asked. In the last fifty days, SCOTUS struck down Trump’s unprecedented tariff program, Congress passed a bipartisan resolution to remove unauthorized military units from hostilities in Iran, the longest government shutdown in U.S. history ended, and the redistricting fight intensified.
The fight takes a while. It is more than just showing up to a ballot box, it’s about waking up and choosing the _better_ path every day; to use one’s voice and power for the sake of ourselves and neighbors. In this crowded primary, there’s only **one** candidate who understands that:_**Elizabeth Dempsey Beggs.**_
In the last 50 days, Elizabeth has worked hard to call voters and knock on doors, run and walk with constituents all across the First District, appeared and had great momentum at candidate forums, initiated a suitcase drive for foster kids, and conducted ads to broadcast the voice of Virginians. On top of that, in the last 50 days, she’s made the daily decision to outright reject corporate donations and dark money bribes.
If this is how it’s been going, I have nothing but enthusiasm to see where the next 50 days of the campaign take us as Elizabeth secures the Democratic nomination and starts the end of Rob Wittman’s years as the First’s representative.
If you’re able, get in the heat of the fight with us and **donate**. Any contribution matters. So, can we count on you for **$50** , or to make a recurring payment over these **last fifty days**.

body:
